text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Picture the head of regulatory reporting at a mid-sized European insurance company. It's a Monday morning. Overnight, the regulator has published a consultation on changes to the reporting templates the company has to file every quarter. Three hundred pages, with annexes, written in the careful, dense language that regulators use.

speaker: JAMES
text: And she has a few questions. Which of these changes affect us? Which numbers do we have to calculate differently? Which systems hold the data? How long do we have? And who in the building is going to read all three hundred pages properly?

speaker: NORA
text: Multiply that by every regulation she deals with, insurance capital rules, accounting standards, sustainability reporting, digital resilience, anti-money laundering, and you start to see why some people describe European financial regulation as a jungle.

speaker: JAMES
text: In fact, that's almost exactly the image a German business publication chose when it profiled today's company in 2023. Its headline, roughly translated, was "Software shows the way through the regulation jungle".

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Last time we looked at Creditinfo and credit bureaus in frontier markets. Today we stay in financial services, but move to Munich, with cleversoft, a company that sells regulatory compliance software to banks, insurers and asset managers.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company announcements, trade press, deal advisers' announcements and the private equity firm's own pages. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number comes from the company, we'll flag it. And nothing here is regulatory, legal or investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And a small note on spelling. The company writes its name in lower case, cleversoft, all one word. It's named after its founder, Florian Clever, which I think is one of the better pieces of founder branding we've come across.

speaker: NORA
text: It's hard to beat. So, James. cleversoft in one sentence.

speaker: JAMES
text: cleversoft is a Munich-based, cloud-based regulatory technology company, often called RegTech, that sells software for supervisory reporting, financial crime prevention, digital advisory compliance and financial messaging to banks, insurers and asset managers, mostly in Europe, and it says it serves more than twelve hundred financial institutions.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because it's in the middle of a fast buy-and-build. Four acquisitions under its current owner since 2024, two of them announced in 2026. And because its core job, reading regulation and turning it into working software, is exactly the kind of job that large language models are getting good at. That's both its best AI opportunity and its biggest AI threat.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. When and where was it founded?

speaker: JAMES
text: The company dates its founding to 2004, and the group traces its roots to an earlier business called Clever Software Solutions, founded in 1999. It's headquartered in Munich. Its other offices, according to a 2026 deal announcement, are in Frankfurt, Luxembourg, Amsterdam, The Hague, Malta, Sofia in Bulgaria, Seville in Spain, Istanbul, Dubai and Kuwait.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a wide spread.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and it reflects the acquisitions. Amsterdam and The Hague come from Dutch businesses it bought, Luxembourg from another, Istanbul and the Gulf from a Turkish acquisition. Sofia is interesting in its own right. In 2023 it had forty-two staff and was described as the second-largest site.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the company?

speaker: JAMES
text: The latest figure is about three hundred and twenty employees, from an October 2026 profile in Wirtschaftsforum, a German business publication. But I want to flag that the public numbers have moved around a lot. In 2023 the private equity firm's announcement said more than a hundred and fifty, and in one place more than a hundred. In late 2024 the company said over a hundred and eighty. And now about three hundred and twenty. Some of that is acquisitions, but the figures from different sources don't line up neatly.

speaker: NORA
text: And customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Same story. Seven hundred in the 2023 announcement. About a thousand in a late 2023 profile. More than twelve hundred in 2025 and 2026. We'll use more than twelve hundred as the current company figure. Revenue isn't public. In the October 2026 profile the company said it has averaged about twenty percent organic growth a year, which is self-reported, so treat it as the company's claim.

speaker: NORA
text: Organic meaning not counting acquisitions.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Growth from selling more to existing and new customers, not from buying other companies. Twenty percent organic would be strong for a business of this kind, if it holds up.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Florian Clever is founder and chief executive, and he's the main public voice of the company. Sascha Wellershoff became chief financial officer in November 2025, succeeding Christoph Reitberger. Gerard McNamara was brought in as chief revenue officer in October 2024. Erwin van Dixhoorn is managing director for supervisory reporting. And when cleversoft bought the Turkish company Fineksus, Fineksus's chief executive, Ahmet Vefik Dincer, joined the executive board.

speaker: NORA
text: Anyone running technology or AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a chief technology officer, chief product officer or AI lead named in public sources. That doesn't mean there isn't one, but it's a gap in the public picture, especially for a software company talking about AI.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the ownership history.

speaker: JAMES
text: Founder-led for its first decade and a half. Then in 2018 Main Capital Partners, a Dutch private equity firm that specialises in software, invested. Under Main Capital, cleversoft started buying. In 2019 it bought SecondFloor, an Amsterdam company. In 2020 BusinessForensics, also Dutch. In 2021 CDDS in Luxembourg. And a company called CW360 in 2023, although we couldn't confirm whether that was just before or just after the change of owner.

speaker: NORA
text: What were those earlier companies?

speaker: JAMES
text: SecondFloor was described in 2019 coverage as an Amsterdam-based rival, and our understanding is that it brought supervisory reporting strength in the Netherlands. For BusinessForensics, CDDS and CW360 we don't have enough detail from our sources to describe their products confidently, so I won't guess. The important point is that by the time the current owner arrived, cleversoft already had a track record of buying and absorbing smaller specialists.

speaker: NORA
text: So Main Capital started the roll-up, and Levine Leichtman continued it.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a fair summary, and it's a common pattern. One private equity owner proves the model works, then sells to another who has the capital and appetite to take it further. For management, the playbook stays similar: find specialists, buy them, integrate, cross-sell. What changes is the scale.

speaker: NORA
text: And then Levine Leichtman.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. In June 2023 Levine Leichtman announced it would invest in cleversoft, buying in from Main Capital, in partnership with management. Terms weren't disclosed. It was the private equity firm's first platform investment in the German-speaking region, which people in the industry call DACH, for Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the fourth platform in that particular fund.

speaker: NORA
text: So about three and a half years into the hold.

speaker: JAMES
text: Roughly, yes. That's the middle of a typical hold. Time enough to have done a few acquisitions and to be deep in integrating them, and still time to make bigger product bets before anyone thinks about a sale.

speaker: NORA
text: You said four acquisitions under the current owner.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. In May 2024, tetralog systems, a Munich company doing digital investment advisory software. By February 2025, the completion of Fineksus, an Istanbul company specialising in financial messaging through the SWIFT network and in anti-money laundering. In May 2026, an agreement to buy FAIT Internet Software, an Austrian digital advisory software company, with closing expected later in the year. And in August 2026, an agreement to buy FS Assist, a British company that does Solvency II reporting for insurers.

speaker: NORA
text: Have the last two closed?

speaker: JAMES
text: We couldn't confirm either. The FS Assist announcement said closing was expected later in August, and one source said the deal was done on the eleventh, but we didn't see a completion notice. So, to be careful: announced, closing not confirmed.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain SWIFT for listeners.

speaker: JAMES
text: SWIFT is the global messaging network that banks use to send payment instructions and other financial messages to each other across borders. Banks need software to create, receive, check and route those messages. Fineksus does that, plus screening those payments for financial crime, which is a natural fit with cleversoft's anti-money laundering work.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the problem cleversoft solves. Why is regulation such a big burden for financial firms?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because there's so much of it, and it keeps changing. A European insurer, for example, has to report its capital position to its regulator under Solvency II, which is the European framework for how much capital insurers must hold against their risks. It has to apply the IFRS 17 accounting standard for insurance contracts. It may have to report on sustainability under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, CSRD. And under DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, it has to show it can withstand technology disruptions and cyber attacks.

speaker: NORA
text: That's four acronyms already.

speaker: JAMES
text: And that's just the insurer. An asset manager deals with the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, SFDR, which governs how funds describe their sustainability credentials. A firm selling investment products to retail customers deals with PRIIPs, which requires short, standardised key information documents. Investment advice falls under MiFID II, the main European rules for investment services. Switzerland has its own equivalent, called FIDLEG, and Germany has its own securities trading law. Pension funds have IORP, a European directive for occupational pension schemes. And everyone deals with anti-money laundering rules.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's take one of those as an example. DORA. What does it actually require?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, DORA is a European Union regulation that has applied since January 2025. It requires financial firms to manage technology risk properly: to have frameworks for identifying and handling information technology risks, to report major incidents to regulators, to test their resilience, and to manage the risks from their technology suppliers. That last part is interesting, because it means banks and insurers have to scrutinise vendors like cleversoft more closely.

speaker: NORA
text: So regulation creates demand for cleversoft, and also raises the bar for cleversoft as a supplier.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. A vendor selling into European financial institutions now has to be able to show its own resilience, security and incident handling. In our view that favours vendors with mature processes and can be hard for very small specialists, which may be one more reason the market is consolidating.

speaker: NORA
text: And sustainability reporting? I've heard that's been in flux.

speaker: JAMES
text: It has, as general background. The European Union introduced extensive sustainability reporting requirements, and there has since been political debate about simplifying them and changing timelines. For vendors, that kind of flux is double-edged. Uncertainty can make customers delay purchases. But every change, including a simplification, still has to be implemented in the software, which is work customers pay for.

speaker: NORA
text: And all of these are in cleversoft's product set?

speaker: JAMES
text: According to its product listings, yes, across its four domains. That breadth is a big part of the pitch. One vendor that can cover several of these regimes, rather than a different specialist for each.

speaker: NORA
text: Why can't firms just do it themselves?

speaker: JAMES
text: Some large firms do build parts in-house. But it's expensive and never-ending. Every regulation comes with detailed technical specifications: which data points, which formats, which validation rules. Regulators update them regularly. If you build in-house, you need a team that reads every update, works out what it means, changes the calculations, tests them and gets them live before the deadline. For a mid-sized insurer or bank, it's usually cheaper to buy software from a vendor who does that once for many clients.

speaker: NORA
text: So the vendor is really selling a promise to keep up.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it exactly. cleversoft calls it its compliance commitment. The company says it implements legal changes in its software and proactively informs customers. And the founder put it this way, in translation: "We don't simply sell software, but show our customers how they can fully implement new regulation."

speaker: NORA
text: That sounds more like a service than a product.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a blend, and in my view that's the heart of the business. The software is the delivery vehicle. The real value is the regulatory expertise built into it, and the ongoing work of keeping it current. That's what customers pay for year after year.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go through the four domains. Start with supervisory reporting.

speaker: JAMES
text: Supervisory reporting is the regular, formal reporting that financial firms send to their regulators. For insurers under Solvency II, that's a set of detailed templates on capital, assets, liabilities and risks. cleversoft's software takes the firm's data, performs the calculations, produces the reports in the required format, runs the validation checks the regulator expects, and helps submit them. FS Assist, the August 2026 deal, adds a Solvency II product called SII Assist, which the deal announcement says is used in the United Kingdom and eighteen countries of the European Economic Area, by about three hundred and fifty European insurers.

speaker: NORA
text: Then financial crime.

speaker: JAMES
text: Financial crime prevention covers anti-money laundering, sanctions screening and fraud. The software monitors transactions for suspicious patterns, screens customers and payments against sanctions lists, and helps investigators manage cases. A product page says its financial crime model constantly improves by learning from suspicious behaviour, though there's no technical detail. And at Sibos 2025, the big annual banking conference, cleversoft and Fineksus presented a joint anti-money laundering and financial crime platform with what they called integrated AI for fraud prevention and real-time compliance.

speaker: NORA
text: Third, digital advisory.

speaker: JAMES
text: Digital advisory and compliance is software that helps banks and wealth managers give investment advice in a way that follows the rules. Checking that a product suits a customer, recording the advice, producing the required disclosures, handling sustainability preferences. That's where tetralog and FAIT fit, both of them advisory software companies.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth, financial messaging.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's mainly Fineksus, the SWIFT messaging work. Creating, validating and routing payment messages, and linking them to financial crime screening.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a common platform underneath?

speaker: JAMES
text: The company describes a proprietary platform called eFrame, with a cloud architecture, and the founder emphasises cloud delivery. How much of each acquired product actually runs on that common platform today, we couldn't tell from public sources. That's an important question for integration and for AI, and we'll come back to it.

speaker: NORA
text: How do customers find cleversoft?

speaker: JAMES
text: The company has said referrals are a major channel. In a market like regulatory software, compliance officers and reporting heads talk to their peers at other firms. A recommendation from someone who has survived a reporting deadline with a vendor carries a lot of weight.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Take the insurer from the cold open. Walk me through what happens when a regulation changes. An invented example.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call the insurer Rheinland Mutual, a mid-sized German insurer, and the head of reporting Katrin. The European insurance regulator publishes an update to the Solvency II reporting templates. Some data points are added, some definitions change, and a few validation rules are tightened. It takes effect for reports in about a year.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What does Katrin do if she has no vendor?
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: She assembles a small project. Someone reads the update in full and writes a summary. Someone compares old and new templates line by line. The actuaries work out which calculations change. IT works out which source systems hold the new data, and whether that data is even captured today. Then they build, test, and hope it works on the first live submission. It takes months, and it pulls her best people away from their day jobs.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And with cleversoft?
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: With a vendor like cleversoft, a lot of that happens centrally, once, for all customers. cleversoft's regulatory team reads the update, works out what changes, updates the templates, calculations and validation rules in the software, tests them, and ships a new release. It also sends customers a note explaining what's changed and what they need to do on their side, for example supply a new data field.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So Katrin's job becomes much smaller.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Much smaller. She checks the note, makes sure her data team can provide the new fields, runs a test submission on the new release, and reviews the results. Instead of a six-month project, it's a few weeks of focused work. That's the value of the compliance commitment.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And where's the time going at cleversoft?
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: In that central regulatory and content team. Reading the regulation, interpreting it, mapping it to the software, building and testing the changes, writing the customer guidance. That's skilled, specialist labour, and it's repeated for every regulation, every update, every jurisdiction. It's exactly the work the founder says AI is now helping with.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Which brings us to AI. But first, the market.
chapter: A new rule, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's look more closely at the acquisition strategy. What's the logic?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, it's to become a single-platform provider across several regulatory domains, so that a bank or insurer can buy more from one vendor. Each acquisition adds either a product domain or a customer base, sometimes both.

speaker: NORA
text: Take them one by one.

speaker: JAMES
text: tetralog, in 2024, adds digital investment advisory, in Germany. Fineksus, completed in 2025, adds SWIFT messaging and anti-money laundering, plus a base in Turkey and access to the Middle East. FAIT, announced in 2026, adds more digital advisory software, in Austria. And FS Assist, announced in August 2026, adds Solvency II reporting and a base of about three hundred and fifty insurers, many of them in the United Kingdom.

speaker: NORA
text: And the plan for FS Assist's customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: cleversoft has said it plans to offer its wider compliance and reporting products to FS Assist's insurers. That's the classic cross-sell. You buy a company with a loyal customer base and a strong product, then introduce those customers to the rest of your portfolio.

speaker: NORA
text: Same for Fineksus?

speaker: JAMES
text: Our inference is yes. Fineksus's anti-money laundering capability can be offered to cleversoft's existing bank customers, and cleversoft's reporting products to Fineksus's customers. The joint platform at Sibos 2025 was an early sign of that. The original plan, at completion, was to finish integrating Fineksus by the end of 2025. We didn't see confirmation of whether that happened on schedule.

speaker: NORA
text: Four deals in about twenty-six months. That's a lot of integration.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and that's the central management challenge. Each acquired company has its own technology, its own data model, its own customers and its own culture. Some are in different countries with different languages. Getting them onto shared platforms, shared processes and a single go-to-market takes years. The more deals you do, the more integration you carry.

speaker: NORA
text: Is the pace likely to continue?

speaker: JAMES
text: The cadence, roughly one deal every six to twelve months, suggests there's a pipeline. That's our inference. RegTech is a fragmented market with lots of small specialists, so there are plenty of potential targets.

speaker: NORA
text: Fineksus stands out as the odd one geographically. Turkey and the Gulf, in a mostly European group.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, and I think it's one of the more interesting deals. It gave cleversoft a base in Istanbul, and with the Dubai and Kuwait offices, a route into the Middle East. Financial crime and payments messaging are needs everywhere, and banks in those regions face strong international pressure on anti-money laundering standards. So it's a way to grow outside Europe with products that travel well, rather than with European reporting products that don't.

speaker: NORA
text: And the reverse? Fineksus products coming into Europe?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the other half of the logic, and the joint platform at Sibos 2025 suggests the two teams were working on exactly that. Whether European banks buy it at scale is one of the things we'd want to see evidence of. That's our view of the strategy, rather than anything the company has spelled out.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the RegTech market?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable figure, so I won't quote one. What we can say is that the demand drivers are strong: a steady stream of new European regulation, tough enforcement on anti-money laundering, and hard reporting deadlines that firms can't miss.

speaker: NORA
text: Who does cleversoft compete with?

speaker: JAMES
text: A data provider, CB Insights, lists several alternatives. We didn't verify their ownership, so I'll describe them only briefly. Regnology does regulatory reporting and data solutions for financial services, and is probably the closest head-to-head competitor in supervisory reporting. LPA, based in Frankfurt and founded in 1999, is described as a RegTech company and is probably the closest German peer. Corlytics, from Dublin, does regulatory intelligence and automated policy compliance, which is closest to cleversoft's regulatory change pitch.

speaker: NORA
text: Others?

speaker: JAMES
text: FundApps, which offers compliance monitoring and reporting software as a service. Kaizen Reporting, based in London, founded in 2013, in compliance and regulatory reporting. Continuity Control, a compliance platform. And H3M Analytics, which describes itself as an AI-driven financial compliance vendor, and which could be an example of an AI-native challenger, though we didn't look into it further.

speaker: NORA
text: How does cleversoft differ?

speaker: JAMES
text: Mainly breadth. Most competitors focus on one or two domains. cleversoft's pitch is coverage across reporting, financial crime, advisory and messaging, from one vendor, with the regulatory expertise built in. The risk with breadth is that each individual product has to be as good as a specialist's, or customers will pick the specialist.

speaker: NORA
text: How sticky is this kind of software? Once a bank picks a vendor, does it stay?

speaker: JAMES
text: Generally, quite sticky, in our understanding of the category. Regulatory reporting software is wired into the firm's data, its calendar of deadlines and its audit trail. Switching vendors means re-mapping data, re-testing every report and taking the risk of getting a submission wrong during the change. Few heads of reporting want that risk unless they're unhappy. That's why renewals and cross-selling tend to matter more than winning brand-new logos.

speaker: NORA
text: Which makes the integration even more important.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does. A customer who is happy with one product is the easiest person to sell a second one to, but only if the second product works smoothly with the first. If buying another cleversoft product feels like buying from a different vendor, the cross-sell advantage shrinks.

speaker: NORA
text: And the big software suites?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, larger vendors with deep pockets can out-invest a private equity-backed roll-up on AI. That's an inference, but it's a real consideration. Whoever builds the best AI for reading and implementing regulation could gain a big advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned regulators themselves are starting to ask about AI.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. A 2026 blog from fina2, which is another vendor in supervisory reporting, so treat it as a vendor view, argues that supervisors now expect AI governance, model lineage and audit trails from firms using AI in reporting. Model lineage means being able to show which model, which version and which data produced a given number. If that's right, it's a demand driver for vendors who can build those controls in.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's take stock. Where is cleversoft with AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: There are three pieces of public evidence. First, the joint anti-money laundering platform with Fineksus at Sibos 2025, presented with integrated AI for fraud prevention and real-time compliance. Second, the product page saying its financial crime model constantly learns from suspicious behaviour. Third, the founder's comments in October 2026.

speaker: NORA
text: What did he say?

speaker: JAMES
text: In the Wirtschaftsforum profile, he said AI speeds up product development and helps analyse regulatory texts, and that it's also used for technical translation. And he was clear that humans remain decisive. AI supports the work, but people make the calls.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a sensible position for a compliance company.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very sensible. If you get a regulatory report wrong, the consequences land on your customer, and then on you. So "AI assists, humans decide" is the right stance, especially at this stage.

speaker: NORA
text: What's missing?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find AI partnerships, AI hires or an AI budget. We didn't find technical detail behind the AI features. And the Sibos platform is a launch claim. We couldn't confirm it's being sold and used at scale. We also didn't find AI-specific governance published, or security certifications, although, as always, that doesn't mean they don't exist.

speaker: NORA
text: What could go wrong with AI reading regulation?

speaker: JAMES
text: The obvious risk is that the model misreads or invents something. Large language models can produce confident text that is subtly wrong. In regulatory work, a missed definition change or a misread threshold could lead to a wrong report. That's why the human review, the tests, and the traceability back to the exact paragraph of the regulation all matter. An AI suggestion that can't be traced to its source shouldn't make it into a release.

speaker: NORA
text: And there's the European AI Act.

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, yes. The EU AI Act sets obligations depending on how risky an AI use is, and some uses in financial services, such as credit scoring, are treated as high risk. Using AI internally to help experts read regulation is likely to be a lower-risk use, but cleversoft's customers will still want to know how AI features in products they buy are governed. Publishing a clear AI policy would help, in our view.

speaker: NORA
text: So how would you characterise it?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, cleversoft is somewhere in the early middle. It has a named AI feature in a core product, in financial crime, and it says it uses AI internally on its most important process, regulatory analysis. But the public evidence is thin, and there's no visible AI leadership. It's further along than some companies we've covered, and less far than its opportunity suggests it should be.

speaker: NORA
text: Why does the internal use matter so much?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because of where cleversoft's costs and value sit. Reading regulation and turning it into software is the company's core work. If AI can make that work significantly faster and more reliable, cleversoft can ship updates sooner, support more regulations with the same team, and improve margins. That's not a side project. It's the engine of the business.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's list the challenges. What keeps leadership up at night, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, integration load. Four acquisitions in about twenty-six months, each with its own technology stack and customers, two of them still closing as of our last information. Combining products, data models and teams across Germany, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria, Turkey and Britain is a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, the AI threat to its own revenue model. Customers pay partly for cleversoft's expertise in reading and implementing regulation. If AI makes that much cheaper for everyone, including competitors and even general-purpose AI vendors, the value of that expertise could be squeezed. That's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, data discipline. The public numbers on staff and customers vary a lot from source to source. That may be just a communications issue, but in our view it can also suggest that the company's internal metrics need tightening, which matters a lot for integration and for a future sale.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, leadership depth. The founder is chief executive and the main public voice. There's a new chief financial officer from late 2025, a new chief revenue officer from 2024, and no visible technology or AI leader. For a company with an AI-heavy future, that's a gap worth filling.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, regulatory cycles. Demand is driven by deadlines. If regulators delay rules, or if the political mood shifts toward simplification, spending can slow. That's our inference, and it cuts both ways, because simplification itself creates change work.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a cultural challenge in a roll-up like this?

speaker: JAMES
text: Definitely. Acquired companies often have proud, specialist teams. A Solvency II expert in Britain, an anti-money laundering engineer in Istanbul and an advisory software developer in Vienna all see the world differently. Getting them to share a platform, a roadmap and an AI approach requires leadership that respects their expertise while insisting on common standards.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's flip to opportunities. If you were on the board, where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: First, cross-selling into the acquired bases. Reporting and compliance products into FS Assist's three hundred and fifty insurers. Anti-money laundering from Fineksus into the bank base. That's the company's own stated plan for FS Assist.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, productise AI-assisted regulatory change. Today, the compliance commitment is part of what customers get. cleversoft could also sell a rules-to-controls capability as a priced module. A tool that reads a new regulation, identifies what changes for that specific customer, maps it to their data and processes, and produces a draft implementation plan.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, geographic expansion. The founder has said the United States is expected to receive more focus. The Middle East and Turkey are already reachable through Fineksus and the Dubai and Kuwait offices.

speaker: NORA
text: The United States is a very different regulatory world.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very different, and I'd be cautious. American rules for insurers and banks differ a lot from European ones, and the market has strong incumbents. The most transferable piece is probably financial crime, where the problems are similar worldwide. That's our view.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, delivery margin. The Sofia office is a substantial site. Moving more build, testing and regulatory content work there, supported by AI, could save real money. Fifth, the new regulation pipeline. The founder sees opportunities in new rules on private retirement provision and in digital, compliant advice. And sixth, continued bolt-on acquisitions.

speaker: NORA
text: And AI in financial crime?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a big one too. As general background, anti-money laundering systems are notorious for false positives. Investigators spend most of their time clearing alerts that turn out to be nothing. AI that reduces false alarms and helps investigators triage faster is now a standard pitch across the industry. cleversoft has a foothold there with the Sibos platform, and it should push to show measurable results.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a data opportunity across all those institutions?

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly, with great care. A vendor that processes regulatory reports for many insurers sees patterns: which validation rules most often fail, which templates cause the most trouble, how long firms take to adopt new requirements. Used in aggregated, anonymised form, and only where contracts and law allow, that could help cleversoft warn customers about common errors before they submit. I'd be very cautious about anything beyond that, because this is confidential supervisory data, and customers would rightly object to it being used loosely. That's our suggestion, not anything the company has proposed.

speaker: NORA
text: One AI bet for the next eighteen months. What is it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: AI-assisted regulatory change. Turning new rules into tested calculations, reporting templates and control steps, with humans signing off. It's the company's own core process, the founder already says AI is helping with it, and it has a clear labour cost and a clear speed benefit. If it works internally, it can also become a product.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's replay the Rheinland Mutual story with that in place.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. The regulator publishes its three-hundred-page update. Within hours, the AI system at cleversoft has read it, compared it to the previous version, and produced a structured list of changes: new data points, changed definitions, new validation rules, effective dates. For each change, it suggests which templates, calculations and code components are affected, and drafts the changes.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And then the humans step in.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. cleversoft's regulatory experts review the list. They correct the system where it misread something, and they make the interpretation calls, which are often genuinely ambiguous. Engineers review the drafted code changes and the tests. And the customer note is drafted automatically and checked by an expert. What used to take weeks of reading and mapping takes days.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And for Katrin?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: She gets the release sooner, with a clearer explanation, and, if cleversoft productises it, a tailored view: here's exactly what changes for Rheinland Mutual, given your products and your data. She has more time to prepare and fewer surprises.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run it? Give me a hundred days.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: First thirty days: pick the domain and set the rules. Choose one regulatory area with frequent updates and a strong internal team, Solvency II reporting is a good candidate, especially with FS Assist joining. Map how the team handles an update today, step by step, and how long each step takes. And set governance from day one: which models are used, how outputs are checked, how every AI suggestion is logged and traceable. If regulators expect model lineage from customers, cleversoft should model it itself.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Then?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days thirty to sixty: test on history. Take several past regulatory updates where the final implementation is known. Run the AI on them. How many changes did it find? How many did it miss? How good were the drafted mappings? This builds the evidence and shows the experts where to trust it and where not to.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And the last stretch?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days sixty to a hundred: run it live, in parallel. On the next real update, run the AI-assisted process alongside the normal one, with the experts comparing. Measure time saved, errors caught and missed. At day one hundred, decide whether to make it the standard internal process for that domain, and which domain comes next. And start shaping the customer-facing version.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: This is where the leadership gap matters. Ideally a senior product or technology leader with authority across the regulatory content team and engineering. If there isn't one, hiring one would be my first move. And a respected regulatory expert as the champion, because the experts have to trust the tool.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: How would the regulatory experts feel about this? Isn't it their job being automated?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a fair worry, and leadership has to address it directly. My view is that in a company growing by around twenty percent a year by its own account and buying more businesses, the realistic outcome isn't fewer experts. It's each expert covering more regulations, faster, with less time spent on reading and copying and more on interpretation and customer guidance. That's a better job. But people need to hear that clearly, and see it in how the programme is run.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And how would you price the customer version?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd start by including faster, clearer updates in the existing subscription, to protect renewals and show value. Then add a premium module for the tailored analysis, the "here's exactly what changes for you" view, priced per regulatory domain. That turns an internal efficiency into new revenue without making customers pay more for what they already get.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And the second-best bet?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: AI triage in the anti-money laundering platform. Let me give a quick example. An invented bank in Luxembourg has investigators facing a queue of alerts every morning. Today they open each one, look up the customer, review the transactions and write a note. With AI triage, each alert arrives with a short summary, the relevant history and a suggested risk level, with the reasons. The investigators work the high-risk ones first and clear obvious false positives much faster. The bank's measures are time per alert and the share of real cases caught. If cleversoft can show those numbers improving at real customers, that's a powerful sales story.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Before we move on, let's do a second walk-through, on the advisory side, since that's where tetralog and FAIT fit. Another invented example.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Picture a private bank in Vienna. An adviser, call him Lukas, is meeting a client who wants to invest an inheritance. Under European investment rules, Lukas has to assess whether the products he recommends suit the client: her knowledge and experience, her financial situation, her goals, her tolerance for risk. He also has to ask about her sustainability preferences. And he has to document all of it and give her the required disclosures.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: That sounds like a lot of paperwork for one conversation.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and in the past a lot of it was literally paperwork. Advisory compliance software turns it into a guided digital process. Lukas works through the questions with the client on a tablet, the system checks which products are suitable, flags any that aren't, records the reasoning, and produces the disclosure documents and the suitability report automatically.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And where could AI fit in?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: In a few places, in our view. Summarising the conversation into the required record, which Lukas then checks. Explaining in plain language why a product does or doesn't fit the client's profile. Checking that product documents and the advice record are consistent. And, on the vendor side, updating the rules engine quickly when the advice regulations change. In every case, the adviser remains responsible for the advice, and the regulator will expect that.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: So the same theme. AI does the drafting and the checking, the human does the judgment.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. And the more regulatory domains cleversoft covers, the more places that pattern applies, which is an argument for building the AI capability once, as a shared platform, rather than separately in each product.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from cleversoft?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four lessons. First, if your product is expertise wrapped in software, AI hits both. It can make your expertise cheaper to deliver, and it can make it cheaper for competitors to copy. The answer is to use it on your own core process first, before someone else does.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, a buy-and-build is only as good as its integration. Buying four companies is the easy part. Making them feel like one company to customers, and run on shared data, is where the value is created. And AI makes this even more important, because AI works best on clean, connected data.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, get your numbers straight. Inconsistent public figures on staff and customers may be harmless, but buyers, investors and customers notice. Clear, consistent metrics are a sign of an organisation in control, and they're the baseline for proving any AI benefit.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, "humans decide" is a strategy, not just a safety line. In high-stakes domains, customers want AI that makes experts faster and better, not AI that replaces them. Building products that make the human checkpoint easy, fast and well documented is a competitive advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: I'll add one from the outside. In compliance, trust compounds.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's well said. Every deadline you help a customer hit builds trust, and that trust drives referrals, which the company says is a major channel. AI that helps hit deadlines more reliably builds on that.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disrupting the revenue model by cutting the cost of reading and implementing rules, weakening the pricing power of the compliance commitment. Two, larger vendors such as Regnology out-investing it on AI. Three, deal execution, with FAIT and FS Assist not confirmed closed and several integrations running in parallel. Four, demand cyclicality, if regulation slows. And five, founder dependence.

speaker: NORA
text: Anything else on the list?

speaker: JAMES
text: One more, in my view. Security. A vendor handling supervisory reports, transaction data and customer screening for financial institutions is an attractive target for attackers. Under DORA, a serious incident at a vendor becomes a serious incident for its customers too. We didn't find published certifications, which doesn't mean they're absent, but strong, visible security is part of what customers will increasingly demand.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: At about three and a half years in, the owner will want to see the acquisitions integrated, cross-selling working and a clear AI story, in time for a future sale. The next eighteen months should show measurable progress on all three.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch for?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, confirmation that FAIT and FS Assist have closed, and early signs of cross-selling into FS Assist's insurers. Second, any named AI product or module, especially for regulatory change. Third, a technology or AI leadership hire. And fourth, any evidence from customers that the AI in the financial crime platform reduces false positives.

speaker: NORA
text: And a bonus?

speaker: JAMES
text: Any move into the United States. That would be a big strategic step, and it would tell you a lot about the company's ambition.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does cleversoft really sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: Keeping up with regulation, so customers don't have to.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Regulatory expertise built into software used by more than twelve hundred institutions, by its own count.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot of integration in flight, and no visible technology or AI leader.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI feature today?

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI in the joint anti-money laundering platform, if it proves out at customers.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: AI-assisted regulatory change, from rule text to tested software, with humans signing off.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace compliance teams?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. Regulators want accountable humans. AI will make those teams faster and more consistent.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a head of regulatory reporting should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Ask your vendors how they use AI to implement regulatory changes, and how they prove it's right.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. It's sitting on the right process for AI. It needs to own it before others do.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. cleversoft is a Munich-based regulatory technology company, founded in 2004 with roots going back to 1999, led by its founder Florian Clever. It sells software for supervisory reporting, financial crime prevention, digital advisory compliance and financial messaging, and says it serves more than twelve hundred financial institutions with about three hundred and twenty staff. Main Capital invested in 2018 and Levine Leichtman bought in during 2023, its first platform in the German-speaking region. Since then it has bought tetralog and Fineksus and agreed to buy FAIT and FS Assist, building a one-vendor platform across several regulatory domains. Its core value is the compliance commitment, keeping customers' software current with changing rules. It has AI in its financial crime platform and says it uses AI to analyse regulatory texts, with humans deciding. The big opportunity is AI-assisted regulatory change, first inside the company and then as a product. The big risks are integration load, AI compressing the value of regulatory expertise, and a thin visible leadership bench on technology.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the wider lesson is that when your business is turning complicated rules into working software, AI is not a feature you add. It's a new way of doing your core job, and you want to be the first to master it.
